'''Sir John Rex Beddington''' (born 13 October 1945)<ref name="whoswho"/> is a British population biologist and senior adviser at the [[Oxford Martin School]], and was previously Professor of Applied Population Biology at [[Imperial College London]], and the UK [[Government Chief Scientific Adviser]] from 2008 until 2013.<ref name="globalcrisis">{{cite news |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/7951838.stm |title=Global crisis 'to strike by 2030' chief scientist John Beddington has warned. |work= BBC News|first=Christine |last=McGourty |date=19 March 2009}}</ref><ref name="wereallgoingtodie">{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/science-environment-21357520 |title=Prof Sir John Beddington warns of floods, droughts and storms – BBC News |publisher=BBC |access-date=6 December 2016}}</ref><ref name="advice">{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/political-science/2013/apr/04/science-art-advice-john-beddington |title=John Beddington: The science and art of effective advice &#124; guardian.co.uk |work=The Guardian |location=London |date=4 April 2013}}</ref>

==Education==
Beddington was educated at [[Monmouth School]] in south-east Wales, close to the English border.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.habs-monmouth.org/en/Monmouth%20School%20Alumni |title=Monmouth School Alumni |archive-date=10 March 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120310094130/http://www.habs-monmouth.org/en/Monmouth%20School%20Alumni |url-status=dead }}</ref> He then attended the [[London School of Economics]], gaining a [[Bachelor of Science|BSc]] degree in economics in 1967, and later an [[Master of Science|MSc]] degree in 1968.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://viewer.zmags.com/static/production.zmags/m0x_pdf_9b4c71f7378a82ac32beef42522c4b62|title=DOD's Civil Service Companion 2009–10, 8th edition|website=viewer.zmags.com|access-date=December 30, 2020}}</ref> In 1973 he was awarded a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] degree from the [[University of Edinburgh]].<ref name="phd">{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|first=John Rex|last=Beddington|title=The Exploitation of Red Deer (Cervus Elaphus L.) in Scotland|publisher=University of Edinburgh|year=1973|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=e0YPcgAACAAJ}}</ref>

==Research and career==
Beddington's research applies biology and economics to the [[sustainable management]] of [[natural resources]].<ref name="royal society bio">{{cite web |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/john-beddington-11063/ |title=John Beddington |publisher=[[The Royal Society]] |access-date=4 January 2021}}</ref>

From 1968 to 1971 Beddington was a research assistant at the University of Edinburgh. Among his first published work was a report analysing a survey of motivations of blood donors which appeared as an appendix to [[Richard Titmuss]]' 1970 book ''The Gift Relationship''.<ref>{{cite book|author=Richard Titmuss|chapter=appendix 6: analysis of blood donor motives by Mr John Beddington|title=The Gift Relationship|year=1970|url=https://www.infectedbloodinquiry.org.uk/sites/default/files/401-700%20copy%2012/401-700%20copy%2012/HSOC0019917%20-%20The%20Gift%20Relationship%20from%20human%20blood%20to%20social%20policy%20-%2001%20Jan%201970.pdf}}</ref> From 1971 to 1984 he was a lecturer in population biology at the [[Department of Biology, University of York|University of York]].<ref name="whoswho"/>

===Oxford Martin School===
Beddington was part of the [[Oxford Martin School]] from May 2013 until 2018. He served as the senior advisor to Professor [[Ian Goldin]], the School's Director. The Oxford Martin School is made up of a community of more than 200 researchers, working to address the most pressing global challenges and opportunities of the 21st century.

===Imperial College London===
Beddington joined Imperial in 1984, was promoted to [[Reader (academic rank)|Reader]] in 1987<ref name="imperialcollege">{{cite web|url=http://www3.imperial.ac.uk/people/j.beddington |title=Home – Professor Sir John Beddington |publisher=Imperial College London |access-date=6 December 2016}}</ref> and was appointed Professor of Applied Population Biology there in 1991.

Beddington has been a specialist in the economics and biology of sustainable management of renewable resources, and has previously advised UK ministers on scientific and environmental issues. He has chaired the [[Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs]]' science advisory panel and the Defence Scientific Advisory Committee, and is a member of the Natural Environmental Research Council.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www3.imperial.ac.uk/people/j.beddington/honoursandawards |title=Honors and awards - J. Beddington|access-date=3 September 2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110517075446/http://www3.imperial.ac.uk/people/j.beddington/honoursandawards |archive-date=17 May 2011 }}</ref> He has also advised the European Commission and the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organisation.

===Chief Scientific Adviser===
On 1 October 2007, it was announced by the Prime Minister [[Gordon Brown]] that Beddington would succeed Professor Sir [[David King (scientist)|David King]] as the [[Chief Scientific Adviser to the UK Government]] with effect from 1 January 2008.<ref>{{cite web|title=New Government Chief Scientific Adviser announced|url=http://www.number10.gov.uk/output/Page13362.asp|publisher=HM Government|access-date=10 January 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071005150416/http://www.number10.gov.uk/output/Page13362.asp|archive-date=5 October 2007|url-status=dead|date=1 October 2007}}</ref> His annual remuneration for this role was £165,000.<ref>{{cite web|title=Top civil servant salary list published |url=http://www.direct.gov.uk/en/Nl1/Newsroom/DG_188114 |date=1 June 2010 |publisher=[[Directgov]] |access-date=14 June 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110611191116/http://www.direct.gov.uk/en/Nl1/Newsroom/DG_188114 |archive-date=11 June 2011 }}</ref> Beddington was closely involved in helping the British government formulate its response to the [[Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster]],<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Grimes|first1=Robin|title=The UK Response to Fukushima and Anglo-Japanese Relations|journal=Science & Diplomacy|date=16 June 2014|volume=3|issue=2|url=http://www.sciencediplomacy.org/perspective/2014/uk-response-fukushima-and-anglo-japanese-relations}}</ref> the [[2010 eruptions of Eyjafjallajökull|eruptions of Icelandic volcanoes]] and [[Hymenoscyphus fraxineus|ash dieback disease in the UK]].<ref name="advice"/><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2013/mar/26/in-praise-of-john-beddington |title=In praise of … John Beddington &#124; The Guardian, Editorial Tuesday 26 March 2013 |location=London |date=26 March 2013}}</ref>
In March 2009 Beddington addressed the [[Sustainable Development]] UK conference warning that the world faced a "[[perfect storm]]" involving food shortages, scarce water and insufficient energy resources. These, he explained, would threaten to led to [[civil disorder|public unrest]] and [[territorial dispute]]s. Mass migration from the worst-affected regions would occur as people flee for more sustainable  regions.<ref name="Sample Perfect Storm">{{cite news |last1=Sample |first1=Ian |last2=correspondent |first2=science |title=World faces 'perfect storm' of problems by 2030, chief scientist to warn |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2009/mar/18/perfect-storm-john-beddington-energy-food-climate |access-date=23 June 2023 |work=The Guardian |issue=18 March 2009 |date=2009}}</ref> "We head into a perfect storm in 2030, because all of these things are operating on the same time frame," he argued.<ref name="Sample Perfect Storm"/> In June 2023 a group of climate scientists argued that they saw this as "prescient".<ref name="NS Earlier collapse">{{cite journal |last1=Willcock |first1=Simon |last2=Cooper |first2=Gregory S. |last3=Addy |first3=John |last4=Dearing |first4=John A. |title=Earlier collapse of Anthropocene ecosystems driven by multiple faster and noisier drivers |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41893-023-01157-x#Sec3 |journal=Nature Sustainability |publisher=Springer Nature Limited |doi=10.1038/s41893-023-01157-x |date=2023|s2cid=259238314 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

====Successor====
In April 2013 Beddington was succeeded by [[Mark Walport]].<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Callaway | first1 = E. | title = Britain names next chief science adviser: Immunologist Mark Walport, head of one of the world's largest biomedical charities, will take on role in 2013.| doi = 10.1038/487020a | pmid = 22763530 | journal = Nature | volume = 487 | issue = 7405 | page = 20 | year = 2012 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | author = Anon| doi = 10.1038/487005b | pmid = 22763508 | title = Good advice: The UK government's latest appointment offers hope for British science. | journal = Nature | volume = 487 | issue = 7405 | year = 2012 | pages = 5–6 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

===Awards and honours===
Professor Beddington was awarded the Heidelberg Award for Environmental Excellence in June 1997, was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] in 2001<ref>{{cite web|url=http://royalsociety.org/about-us/fellowship/fellows|title=Royal Society Fellows 1660-date|publisher=The Royal Society|access-date=20 July 2010|location=London}}</ref> and was appointed [[Companion of the Order of St Michael and St George]] (CMG) by Queen Elizabeth II in 2004, in recognition of his services to fisheries science and management.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = May | first1 = R. M. | last2 = Beddington | first2 = J. R. | author-link2 = John Beddington| last3 = Clark | first3 = C. W. | last4 = Holt | first4 = S. J. | last5 = Laws | first5 = R. M. | title = Management of Multispecies Fisheries | doi = 10.1126/science.205.4403.267 | journal = Science | volume = 205 | issue = 4403 | pages = 267–277 | year = 1979 | pmid =  17747032| bibcode = 1979Sci...205..267M | s2cid = 36710281 }}</ref> He was also appointed an Honorary [[Fellow]]<ref name="List of Fellows"/> of the [[Royal Academy of Engineering]]<ref name="List of Fellows"/> in 2012 and was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]]<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.rse.org.uk/fellow/john-beddington/|title=Sir John Rex Beddington KB CMG HonFREng FRS FRSE - The Royal Society of Edinburgh|work=The Royal Society of Edinburgh|access-date=2018-06-28|language=en-GB}}</ref> in 2011.

In July 2014, he was recognised by the Government of Japan for his contributions to strengthening the co-operation between Japan and the UK in the areas of science and technology.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.oxfordmartin.ox.ac.uk/news/201407_Beddington_Honour |title=Japanese honour for Sir John Beddington &#124; Oxford Martin School |publisher=University of Oxford |access-date=6 December 2016}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Beddington was [[Knight Bachelor|knighted]] in the 2010 Birthday Honours.<ref>{{London Gazette |issue=59446 |date=12 June 2010 |page=1 |supp=y }}</ref> He was married to Sarah West from 1968 until their divorce in 1972. They have one son. In 1973, he married social policy professor [[Sally Baldwin]]. They divorced in 1979, and have one daughter, Emma Beddington, journalist at ''[[The Guardian]]''. He married his current spouse, Caroline Hiller, in 1990.<ref name="whoswho"/>
